messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Graphical representation of covariance residuals?
parts:
Is there a strong package for rendering covariance residuals graphically? The corrplot::corrplot() function, with is.corr=F, creates some colorful graphs, but I'm not sure the rendering is more evocative than the numbers themselves, though I am just starting to experiment. Thanks for any ideas.

library(lavaan)
library(corrplot)
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
mat<-lavResiduals(fit,type="raw")
corrplot(mat$cov,is.corr=F)

messages.author: ff3a366aa7a9b488
messages.subject: Re: Graphical representation of covariance residuals?
parts:
Hi Ed,

it depends on what you want to achieve. There are many packages to graph correlation matrices and the like. As far as I can see, these packages all do more or less the same thing.

A nice alternative might be a heatmap with r::plotly. You have to tinker a bit, but the output is "interactive" (mouseover the diagram) and there are a lot of formatting options: https://plotly.com/r/reference/heatmap/

Here is an example:

library(lavaan)
library(plotly)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)

mat <- lavResiduals(fit,type="raw")

mat$cov[upper.tri(mat$cov)] <- FALSE                   # If you want to get rid of the upper triangular matrix ...
mat <- round(mat$cov[nrow(mat$cov):1, ], 3)

create.colorscale <- function(sm, mat) {
  m          <- data.frame(val = as.numeric(unique(c(mat))))
  m$rescaled <- scales::rescale(m$val)
  m          <- m[order(m$rescaled),]
  colors     <- data.frame(val = numeric(0), color = character(0))
 
  lower <- m[m$val <= 0,]
  upper <- m[m$val > 0,]
 
  cols <- c(
    1 - lower$val / min(lower$val),
    1 - upper$val / max(upper$val)
  )^sm
 
  r <- as.integer((cols + (1 - cols) * 0.9) * 255)
  g <- as.integer((cols + (1 - cols) * 0.1) * 255)
  b <- as.integer((cols + (1 - cols) * 0.1) * 255)
 
  setNames(data.frame(m$rescaled, paste0("rgb(", r, ",", g, ",", b, ")")), NULL)
}

fig <- plot_ly(
  z = mat,
  x = colnames(mat),
  y = rownames(mat),
  type = "heatmap",
  xgap = 0,
  ygap = 0,
  colorscale = create.colorscale(0.4, mat)
)

fig

The ceate.colorscale function is written quick and dirty. You can certainly be creative here, depending on how you want the output to be. In the above example, the color gradient is more or less continuous. The greater the deviation from zero, the redder the gradient. Here is an example for categories (beware my choice of color is really ugly and the categories might be meaningless - sorry):

library(lavaan)
library(plotly)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)

mat <- lavResiduals(fit,type="raw")

mat <- round(mat$cov[nrow(mat$cov):1, ], 3)


create.colorscale <- function(thresholds, mat) {
  m          <- data.frame(val = as.numeric(unique(c(mat))))
  m$rescaled <- scales::rescale(m$val)
  m          <- m[order(m$rescaled),]
  colors    <- data.frame(val = numeric(0), color = character(0))
 
  for(t in thresholds) {
   
    if(t[[1]][1] == -Inf) v1 <- 0
    else {
      row <- nrow(m[m$val < t[[1]][1],])
      v1 <- m[row, "rescaled"] + 0.0001
    }
    if(t[[1]][2] == Inf) v2 <- 1
    else {
      row <- nrow(m[m$val < t[[1]][2],])
      v2 <- m[row, "rescaled"] + 0.0001
    }
    colors <- rbind(
      colors,
      cbind(val = v1, color = t[[2]][1]),
      cbind(val = v2, color = t[[2]][1])
    )
  }
  setNames(data.frame(as.numeric(colors[, 1]), colors[, 2]), NULL)
}


thresholds <- list(
  list(
    c(-Inf, -0.1),
    "rgb(182,14,48)"
  ),
  list(
    c(-0.1, 0.0),
    "rgb(128,255,72)"
  ),
  list(
    c(-0.001, 0.001),
    "rgb(255,255,255)"
  ),
  list(
    c(0.001, 0.1),
    "rgb(179,249,149)"
  ),
  list(
    c(0.1, Inf),
    "rgb(244,165,194)"
  )
)

fig <- plot_ly(
  z = mat,
  x = colnames(mat),
  y = rownames(mat),
  type = "heatmap",
  xgap = 2,
  ygap = 2,
  colorscale = create.colorscale(thresholds, mat)
)

fig

Again, the create.colorscale function is written quick and dirty ^^

HTH

Christian

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Graphical representation of covariance residuals?
parts:
Ed,
Perhaps you can anticipate my answer before you read it but my two go-to graphs for residuals are decidedly low tech.  I like heat maps as Christian suggested.  However, the first thing that I look at is usually a stem plot of the unique off-diagonal residuals.

> stem(r[lower.tri(r, diag=FALSE)]) # r = residual matrix

  The decimal point is 2 digit(s) to the left of the |

  -2 | 042
  -0 | 973975432
   0 | 000000000000000125503
   2 | 44459
   4 | 1001
   6 | 232

Part of the reason that I like this plot is that it emphasizes what the matrix does not, the univariate distribution of the residuals themselves.  That makes it easier to spot outliers and bimodal distributions.  Once I spot the values of interest here, I can go back to the matrix to look up the variables involved in producing them.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

Christian and Keith--
Thank you both. These are terrific suggestions. I am thinking about my students this Fall. The chi-square is not a black box, but it can seem that way if you can't really intuit the residuals matrix. Instead of telling my students to just take someone's word regarding what fit information to value, I'd love to help them trace back to the element-by-element results--granting the limitations of many to one. I feel like there should be a graphical way to get at the uncertainty around the individual covariance residuals.

messages.subject: Re: Graphical representation of covariance residuals?
parts:
I did not start this thread but I would like to thank Christian and Keith too. I also had the same question Ed raised. I do agree that we, students and researchers, should pay more attention to the residuals matrix. However, except for some toy examples or models with very few variables, practically it is not easy to make sense of the residuals of a matrix with, say, nine or more variables, e.g., the commonly used sample dataset for CFA with nine items ("HS.model" in the example). It would be great to have some graphical tools to help us examine the residuals matrix.

Thanks again.

-- Shu Fai

messages.author: bc810b1d0900407f
messages.subject: Re: Graphical representation of covariance residuals?
parts:
For a model with many variables, Keith's approach is a useful one. This is an illustration of combining stem plot with corrplot():

Ed's example:
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-15
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
library(corrplot)
#> corrplot 0.92 loaded

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
mat <- lavResiduals(fit,type = "raw")

mat_z <- mat$cov.z

First, examine the stem plot as suggested by Keith (or any similar univariate plot):

# Stem plot
stem(mat_z[lower.tri(mat_z, diag = FALSE)])
#> 
#>   The decimal point is at the |
#> 
#>   -4 | 21
#>   -3 | 87
#>   -2 | 6300
#>   -1 | 994110
#>   -0 | 87664333
#>    0 | 799
#>    1 | 24567
#>    2 | 277
#>    3 | 5
#>    4 | 18

Decide a cutoff value from the the stem plot:

# Form indices to select rows and columns with absolute values > 4.1
i1 <- abs(mat_z) > 4.1
i2 <- apply(i1, 1, any)

Use the index vector to examine only rows and columns with extreme values::

# Print or plot the sub matrix
round(mat_z[i2, i2], 3)
#>        x3     x5     x7     x8     x9
#> x3  0.000 -4.157 -1.858 -0.300  3.518
#> x5 -4.157  0.000 -0.842 -1.099  1.701
#> x7 -1.858 -0.842  0.000  4.823 -2.325
#> x8 -0.300 -1.099  4.823  0.000 -4.132
#> x9  3.518  1.701 -2.325 -4.132  0.000
corrplot(abs(mat_z[i2, i2]), is.corr = FALSE)
The last step can be replaced by other methods, such as the heat map Christian introduced.

Ideally, we want to examine the full matrix. However, it is not unusual to have a model with 15 or even 20 variables. This approach may be more practical for a large matrix, at least for preliminary analysis.

Regards,
Shu Fai Cheung (張樹輝)

To quickly get an idea of the 'largest' values among the covariance
residuals, you can use

library(lavaan)
example(cfa)

lavResiduals(fit, output = "table")

and to get the stem() plot:

stem( lavResiduals(fit, output = "table")$res )

Yves.

Part of the reason that I like this plot is that it emphasizes what the matrix does not, the univariate distribution of the residuals themselves.  That makes it easier to spot outliers and bimodal distributions.  Once I spot the values of interest here, I can go back to the matrix to look up the variables involved in producing them.

parts:
Ed,
That is an interesting question.  At first blush, it seems to me that the graph is the easy part.  The hard part is obtaining a numeric measure of uncertainty to incorporate into the graph.  For uncertainty due to sampling variation, I like Cleveland dot plots with error bars, which are easily constructed using the points(x,y) and arrows(lb,y,ub,y,angle=90, code=3, ...) functions.  Put the values of the estimate on the horizontal axis and different estimates (or sets thereof) on different rows of the vertical axis.  Draw the error bars first so that the points go on top.  Use colors to distinguish estimates on the same row, if any.

It seems to me that the main challenge to what you are describing is that, unlike a chi-square for a frequency table or contingency table, each element of the covariance matrix does not make an independent contribution to the chi-quare (as I understand it).  The same estimated parameter can impact multiple implied covariances and I would expect estimates of implied covariances to be associated across samples from the same population.  Unless I am missing something, that makes it more challenging to trace uncertainty about a single covariance back to model fit.  You might have to look at the covariance matrix of the implied covariances, which would get very large very quickly as the number of variables increases and might be too much for students in an introductory course.  Off the top of my head, I wonder whether students might obtain more insight from simply seeing histograms of various covariances and fit measures from a single-condition simulation study.

I would be interested to hear what you come up with.

Keith
